claim: Certain bacteria demonstrate the ability to target and colonize the tumor microenvironment.
source: Certain bacteria demonstrate the ability to target and colonize the tumor microenvironment, a characteristic that positions them as innovative carriers for delivering various therapeutic agents in cancer therapy.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: E. coli colonized in tumors notably upregulated processes related to ferric ions, including enterobactin biosynthesis and iron homeostasis, compared to E. coli cultivated in rich medium.
source: Compared to E. coli cultivated in the rich medium, we found that E. coli colonized in tumors notably upregulated the processes related to ferric ions, including the enterobactin biosynthesis and iron homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS/MS proteomic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The tumor is an iron-deficient environment to E. coli.
source: This finding indicated that the tumor is an iron-deficient environment to E. coli.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the proteomic data showing upregulation of iron-related proteins.

claim: The colonization of E. coli in the tumor led to an increased expression of lipocalin 2 (LCN2).
source: We also found that the colonization of E. coli in the tumor led to an increased expression of lipocalin 2 (LCN2), a host protein that can sequester the enterobactin.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS analysis data shown in Figure 1g.

claim: LCN2 is a host protein that can sequester enterobactin.
source: We also found that the colonization of E. coli in the tumor led to an increased expression of lipocalin 2 (LCN2), a host protein that can sequester the enterobactin.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about LCN2 function.

claim: The IroA cluster enables E. coli to synthesize glycosylated enterobactin, which creates steric hindrance to avoid LCN2 sequestration.
source: By introducing the IroA cluster, the E. coli synthesizes the glycosylated enterobactin, which creates steric hindrance to avoid the LCN2 sequestration.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing resistance to LCN2 and established knowledge about the IroA cluster function.

claim: IroA-E. coli showed enhanced resistance to LCN2.
source: The IroA-E. coli showed enhanced resistance to LCN2 and significantly improved the anti-tumor activity in mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: IroA-E. coli significantly improved anti-tumor activity in mice.
source: The IroA-E. coli showed enhanced resistance to LCN2 and significantly improved the anti-tumor activity in mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from multiple mouse tumor models shown in Figure 3.

claim: Mice cured by IroA-E. coli treatment became resistant to tumor re-challenge, indicating the establishment of immunological memory.
source: Moreover, the mice cured by the IroA-E. coli treatment became resistant to the tumor re-challenge, indicating the establishment of immunological memory.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from tumor re-challenge studies shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Bacterial therapy has re-emerged as a promising modality for cancer treatment, building on the pioneering works of William Coley in the late 19th century.
source: Bacterial therapy has re-emerged as a promising modality for cancer treatment, building on the pioneering works of William Coley in the late 19th century (Carlson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Carlson et al., 2020.

claim: Bacteria offer active tumor targeting as an advantage over traditional cancer treatments.
source: As a living therapeutic agent, bacteria offer several advantages over traditional cancer treatments, including (1) active tumor targeting (Yamamoto et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2023)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yamamoto et al., 2016 and Kim et al., 2023.

claim: Bacteria offer tumor colonization as an advantage over traditional cancer treatments.
source: As a living therapeutic agent, bacteria offer several advantages over traditional cancer treatments, including (1) active tumor targeting (Yamamoto et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2023), (2) tumor colonization (Westphal et al., 2008; Weibel et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Westphal et al., 2008 and Weibel et al., 2008.

claim: Bacteria offer immune system stimulation as an advantage over traditional cancer treatments.
source: As a living therapeutic agent, bacteria offer several advantages over traditional cancer treatments, including (1) active tumor targeting (Yamamoto et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2023), (2) tumor colonization (Westphal et al., 2008; Weibel et al., 2008), (3) immune system stimulation (Qiu et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2023)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Qiu et al., 2020 and Yang et al., 2023.

claim: Bacteria offer great engineerability for customized functionalities as an advantage over traditional cancer treatments.
source: As a living therapeutic agent, bacteria offer several advantages over traditional cancer treatments, including (1) active tumor targeting (Yamamoto et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2023), (2) tumor colonization (Westphal et al., 2008; Weibel et al., 2008), (3) immune system stimulation (Qiu et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2023), and (4) great engineerability for customized functionalities (Gurbatri et al., 2020; Hu et al., 2022; Canale et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gurbatri et al., 2020, Hu et al., 2022, and Canale et al., 2021.

claim: The tumor microenvironment provides unique cues such as hypoxia, low pH values, and immune suppressors.
source: The tumor microenvironment (TME) provides unique cues, such as hypoxia, low pH values, and immune suppressors, which facilitate the selective targeting and colonization of certain bacteria, including E. coli (Ryan et al., 2009; Flentie et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ryan et al., 2009 and Flentie et al., 2012.

claim: The molecular physiology of E. coli has been extensively studied under well-controlled laboratory conditions.
source: While the molecular physiology of E. coli has been extensively studied under well-controlled laboratory conditions (Han and Lee, 2006; Mateus et al., 2020), it is unclear how E. coli adapts to the nutrition-limited and immune-responsive environment in tumors.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Han and Lee, 2006 and Mateus et al., 2020.

claim: It is unclear how E. coli adapts to the nutrition-limited and immune-responsive environment in tumors.
source: While the molecular physiology of E. coli has been extensively studied under well-controlled laboratory conditions (Han and Lee, 2006; Mateus et al., 2020), it is unclear how E. coli adapts to the nutrition-limited and immune-responsive environment in tumors.
evidence: This is a statement of the knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: Nutritional immunity is employed by the host organism through restricting the availability of essential nutrients to invading pathogens.
source: Nutritional immunity is employed by the host organism through restricting the availability of essential nutrients to the invading pathogens (Weinberg, 1975; Murdoch and Skaar, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Weinberg, 1975 and Murdoch and Skaar, 2022.

claim: Humans have evolved specialized proteins to chelate trace minerals such as iron, zinc, and manganese, keeping their free-form concentrations at very low levels within the body.
source: For example, humans have evolved specialized proteins to chelate trace minerals, such as iron, zinc, and manganese, keeping their free-form concentrations at very low levels within the body (Andrews and Schmidt, 2007; Kambe et al., 2015; Roth et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Andrews and Schmidt, 2007, Kambe et al., 2015, and Roth et al., 2013.

claim: Bacteria have developed a variety of siderophores to acquire ferric ions from the host.
source: For instance, a variety of siderophores are developed by bacteria to acquire ferric ions from the host (Kramer et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kramer et al., 2020.

claim: Humans have evolved siderophore-sequestering proteins such as LCN2 for bacterial inhibition.
source: Intriguingly, humans have further adapted by evolving siderophore-sequestering proteins, such as LCN2, for bacterial inhibition (Singh et al., 2015; Bachman et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Singh et al., 2015 and Bachman et al., 2009.

claim: There are many more proteins enriched in the rich medium than in the tumor condition for E. coli.
source: Not surprisingly, there are many more proteins enriched in the rich medium than in the tumor condition.
evidence: This is supported by the Venn diagram and volcano plot data shown in Figure 1a and b.

claim: The Venn diagram and volcano blot revealed hundreds of protein IDs enriched in the rich medium condition.
source: The Venn diagram and the volcano blot revealed hundreds of protein IDs enriched in the rich medium condition (Figure 1a and b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1a and b.

claim: Many proteins enriched in rich medium are associated with biosynthetic processes, cell division, and energy production.
source: The Gene Ontology (GO)-term analysis revealed that many of these proteins are associated with the machineries of biosynthetic processes, cell division, and energy production (Figure 1c)
evidence: This is supported by GO-term analysis data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: E. coli was under a highly proliferative state in the rich medium.
source: The Gene Ontology (GO)-term analysis revealed that many of these proteins are associated with the machineries of biosynthetic processes, cell division, and energy production (Figure 1c), reflecting that the E. coli was under a highly proliferative state in the rich medium.
evidence: This is an inference from the GO-term analysis data.

claim: 71 proteins were preferentially expressed in the tumor condition over the rich medium condition.
source: Interestingly, there were also 71 proteins that were preferentially expressed in the tumor condition over the rich medium condition.
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data analysis.

claim: Many proteins preferentially expressed in tumors are involved in enterobactin synthesis and iron ion homeostasis.
source: The GO-term analysis and the hierarchical clustering revealed that many of these proteins are involved in the processes of enterobactin synthesis and iron ion homeostasis (Figure 1d and e, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by GO-term analysis and hierarchical clustering data shown in Figure 1d, e, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Individual proteins in enterobactin synthesis and iron ion homeostasis processes were markedly up-regulated in the tumor condition.
source: Figure 1f showed that the individual proteins in these two processes were markedly up-regulated in the tumor condition.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: Proteins involved in enterobactin synthesis and iron homeostasis are tightly controlled by the iron sensing system in E. coli and only become up-regulated under iron deficiency stress.
source: These proteins are known to be tightly controlled by the iron sensing system in E. coli, and only become up-regulated under the stress of iron deficiency (Seo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Seo et al., 2014.

claim: LCN2 possesses a specialized pocket to bind and sequester enterobactin.
source: It is worth mentioning that while enterobactin facilitates the uptake of ferric ions into bacteria, the host immune cells can counteract by secreting a protein called LCN2, which possesses a specialized pocket to bind and sequester enterobactin (Fischbach et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fischbach et al., 2006.

claim: A significant up-regulation of LCN2 expression was observed in tumors with E. coli inoculation.
source: Indeed, we observed a significant up-regulation of LCN2 expression in the tumors with E. coli inoculation (Figure 1g).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 1g.

claim: All three iron chelators (deferoxamine, ciclopirox, and VLX600) showed high cytotoxicity toward cancer cells.
source: All three chelators showed high cytotoxicity toward the cancer cells, suggesting the essential role of irons for the survival of mammalian cells (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: E. coli can better tolerate iron chelators at relatively high concentrations compared to cancer cells.
source: On the other hand, E. coli can better tolerate these iron chelators at relatively high concentrations.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: VLX600 was the most potent drug against cancer cells with an IC50 of 0.33 μM.
source: Among them, VLX600 was the most potent drug against the cancer cells (IC50=0.33 μM) and provided the largest therapeutic window (280-fold difference) between the cancer cells and E. coli.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: VLX600 provided the largest therapeutic window (280-fold difference) between cancer cells and E. coli.
source: Among them, VLX600 was the most potent drug against the cancer cells (IC50=0.33 μM) and provided the largest therapeutic window (280-fold difference) between the cancer cells and E. coli.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Cyclic di-GMP (CDG) can block the binding between LCN2 and enterobactin, restoring the functionality of enterobactin.
source: It has been reported that cyclic di-GMP (CDG) can block the binding between LCN2 and enterobactin, therefore, restoring the functionality of enterobactin (Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2015.

claim: The addition of CDG can enhance bacteria survival in the presence of LCN2.
source: In our bacterial culture study, we validated that the addition of CDG can enhance bacteria survival in the presence of LCN2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: E. coli transformed with the DGC plasmid actively synthesized CDG and secreted it into the supernatant.
source: We showed that the E. coli transformed with the DGC plasmid (hereafter referred to DGC-E. coli) actively synthesized CDG and secreted it into the supernatant as detected by the LC/MS-MS mass spectrometry (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: CDG is a potent ligand for the STING pathway, which can stimulate anti-tumor immunity.
source: It is worth noting that CDG is also a potent ligand for the STING pathway, which can stimulate anti-tumor immunity (Diner et al., 2013; Krasteva and Sondermann, 2017; Chattopadhyay et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Diner et al., 2013, Krasteva and Sondermann, 2017, and Chattopadhyay et al., 2020.

claim: DGC-E. coli supernatant enhanced IFN-β secretion by macrophages, indicating activation of the STING pathway by CDG.
source: When applying the DGC-E. coli supernatant to the macrophages, the macrophages enhanced the IFN-β secretion, indicating the activation of the STING pathway by CDG (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: VLX600 monotherapy only marginally suppressed tumor growth compared to PBS control.
source: The VLX600 monotherapy only marginally suppressed the tumor growth as compared to the PBS control (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: DGC-E. coli monotherapy inhibited tumor progression but did not show superior efficacy than wild-type E. coli without DGC plasmid transformation.
source: The DGC-E. coli monotherapy, although inhibited the tumor progression to a certain degree, did not show superior efficacy than the wild-type E. coli without the DGC plasmid transformation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: The combination of DGC-E. coli and VLX600 showed significantly improved efficacy compared to individual mono-therapies.
source: Strikingly, the combination of DGC-E. coli and VLX600 showed significantly improved efficacy as compared to the individual mono-therapies.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2e and f.

claim: 2 out of 4 mice achieved complete remission with the combination of DGC-E. coli and VLX600.
source: The tumor sizes were greatly suppressed, and 2 out of 4 mice achieved complete remission (Figure 2e and f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2e and f.

claim: The combination of wild-type E. coli and VLX600 did not result in improved activity, indicating that CDG expression contributed to bacteria's synergism with VLX600.
source: Of note, the combination of the wild-type E. coli and VLX600 did not result in such an improved activity, indicating that the CDG expression contributed to bacteria's synergism with the iron-chelating VLX600.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and inference from the comparison of treatment groups.

claim: The combination of CDG-expressing bacteria and VLX600 established robust anticancer adaptive immunity.
source: The combination of CDG-expressing bacteria and VLX600 also established robust anticancer adaptive immunity as the mice cured by the combinatorial therapy showed no tumor development in a rechallenge study (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Some pathogenic E. coli strains carry a gene cluster called IroA, which consists of five genes to perform enterobactin glycosylation and processing.
source: Some pathogenic E. coli strains carry a gene cluster called IroA, which consists of five genes to perform enterobactin glycosylation and processing.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the IroA cluster.

claim: The sugars on enterobactin create steric hindrance to the LCN2 pocket, thereby abolishing LCN2 binding.
source: The sugars on the enterobactin create steric hindrance to the LCN2 pocket, thereby abolishing LCN2 binding.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about glycosylated enterobactin function.

claim: E. coli without the IroA plasmid transformation (WT-E. coli) was sensitive to LCN2.
source: Figure 3a shows that the E. coli without the IroA plasmid transformation (referred as WT-E. coli) was sensitive to LCN2
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: E. coli transformed with the IroA plasmid (IroA-E. coli) was significantly more resistant to LCN2 than WT-E. coli.
source: Figure 3a shows that the E. coli without the IroA plasmid transformation (referred as WT-E. coli) was sensitive to LCN2, whereas the E. coli transformed with the IroA plasmid (referred as IroA-E. coli) was significantly more resistant to LCN2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: IroA-E. coli showed stronger potency in acquisition of iron ions than WT-E. coli while LCN2 was present in the environment.
source: The IroA-E. coli also showed stronger potency in acquisition of the iron ions than the WT-E. coli while the LCN2 was presented in the environment (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Enterobactin extracted from IroA-E. coli was more cytotoxic to cancer cells than that extracted from WT E. coli.
source: In line with this observation, we found that the enterobactin (including the glycosylated form) extracted from the IroA-E. coli was more cytotoxic to the cancer cells than that extracted from the WT E. coli (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: IroA-E. coli was significantly more efficacious than WT-E. coli in mouse models of colon, breast, and melanoma cancers.
source: In mouse models of colon, breast, and melanoma cancers, the IroA-E. coli was significantly more efficacious than the WT-E. coli.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3d-j.

claim: 6 out of 10 mice treated by IroA-E. coli achieved complete remission in the MC38 mouse colon cancer model.
source: In a MC38 mouse colon cancer model, 6 out of 10 mice treated by IroA-E. coli achieved complete remission, whereas none of the mice treated by the WT-E. coli experienced a cure (Figure 3d–f, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3d-f and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: None of the mice treated by WT-E. coli experienced a cure in the MC38 mouse colon cancer model.
source: In a MC38 mouse colon cancer model, 6 out of 10 mice treated by IroA-E. coli achieved complete remission, whereas none of the mice treated by the WT-E. coli experienced a cure (Figure 3d–f, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3d-f and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: LCN2 expression has been shown to elevate the aggressiveness of breast cancer.
source: It should be pointed out LCN2 expression has been shown to elevate the aggressiveness of breast (Yang et al., 2009), melanoma (Adler et al., 2023), and colon cancers (Chaudhary et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2009.

claim: LCN2 expression has been shown to elevate the aggressiveness of melanoma.
source: It should be pointed out LCN2 expression has been shown to elevate the aggressiveness of breast (Yang et al., 2009), melanoma (Adler et al., 2023), and colon cancers (Chaudhary et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Adler et al., 2023.

claim: LCN2 expression has been shown to elevate the aggressiveness of colon cancers.
source: It should be pointed out LCN2 expression has been shown to elevate the aggressiveness of breast (Yang et al., 2009), melanoma (Adler et al., 2023), and colon cancers (Chaudhary et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chaudhary et al., 2021.

claim: Bacterial burden was undetectable in the blood for both WT-E. coli and IroA-E. coli after intravenous administration.
source: For both WT-E. coli and IroA-E. coli, bacterial burden was undetectable in the blood.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3k.

claim: IroA-E. coli did not adversely affect the immune system within the circulatory system compared to WT-E. coli.
source: Additionally, whole blood cell analysis indicated that IroA-E. coli did not adversely affect the immune system within the circulatory system compared to WT-E. coli.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3l.

claim: By day 7, all treatment groups had comparable blood cell counts to the untreated groups.
source: By day 7, all treatment groups had comparable blood cell counts to the untreated (UT) groups.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3l.

claim: IroA-E. coli could enhance anti-tumor treatment without incurring additional risks of bacteremia or sepsis relative to WT-E. coli.
source: These findings demonstrate that IroA-E. coli could enhance anti-tumor treatment without incurring additional risks of bacteremia or sepsis relative to WT-E. coli.
evidence: This is an inference from the safety data presented.

claim: Many proteins enriched in WT-E. coli colonized in tumors belong to the enterobactin biosynthesis process and iron homeostasis.
source: The GO-term analysis revealed that the many proteins enriched in WT-E. coli belong to the enterobactin biosynthesis process and the iron homeostasis.
evidence: This is supported by GO-term analysis of proteomic data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: All proteins involved in enterobactin biosynthesis and iron homeostasis were expressed at a much higher level in WT-E. coli than in IroA-E. coli when colonized in tumors.
source: Figure 4b and Figure 4c showed the fold changes of the individual proteins in these two terms. Strikingly, all of these proteins were expressed at a much higher level in WT-E. coli than in IroA-E. coli.
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 4b and c.

claim: IroA-E. coli was less stressed by the iron-deficient environment in the TME.
source: These results suggest that IroA-E. coli was less stressed by the iron-deficient environment in the TME, which is in accordance with IroA-E.coli's superior iron-scavenging ability from the glycosylated enterobactin.
evidence: This is an inference from the proteomic data showing lower expression of iron-stress proteins.

claim: Two iron-related proteins in mice, transferrin and transferrin receptor, were elevated in the IroA-E. coli treatment compared to the WT-E. coli treatment.
source: We found that two iron-related proteins in mice, transferrin and transferring receptor, were elevated in the IroA-E. coli treatment as compared to the WT-E. coli treatment (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Transferrin and transferrin receptor are known to be up-regulated when cells sense a lack of iron in the environment.
source: These two proteins are known to be up-regulated when the cells sense a lack of iron in the environment (Ponka and Lok, 1999; Theil, 1990; Ponka et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ponka and Lok, 1999, Theil, 1990, and Ponka et al., 2015.

claim: The potent acquisition of ferric ion by IroA-E. coli posed an iron-deficient stress to the host cells.
source: Our finding corroborates a competitive scenario between the host cells and E. coli where the potent acquisition of ferric ion by IroA-E. coli posed an iron-deficient stress to the host cells.
evidence: This is an inference from the proteomic data showing elevated transferrin and transferrin receptor in host cells.

claim: The absence of tumor growth upon rechallenge indicates the establishment of robust anticancer adaptive immunity.
source: The absence of tumor growth upon rechallenge indicates the establishment of robust anticancer adaptive immunity (Figure 5a)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: TILs, especially CD8+ T cells, were elevated in the IroA-E. coli group compared to the WT-E. coli group.
source: We found that the TILs, especially the CD8+ T cells, were elevated in the IroA-E. coli group compared to the WT-E. coli group (Figure 5b)
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The enhanced CD8+ T cell infiltration can be attributed to the prolonged intratumoral colonization by the IroA-E. coli.
source: The enhanced CD8+ T cell infiltration can be attributed to the prolonged intratumoral colonization by the IroA-E. coli (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), which can confer sustained immune stimulation for immune cell recruitment.
evidence: This is an inference supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The anti-tumor activity of IroA-E. coli was partially weakened upon anti-CD8 depletion.
source: We further performed a CD8+ T-cell depletion study, which showed that the anti-tumor activity of IroA-E. coli was partially weakened upon anti-CD8 depletion (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The robust tumor suppression by IroA-E. coli therapy can be attributed in part to the elicitation of tumor-specific cytotoxic T cells.
source: These results demonstrate that the robust tumor suppression by the IroA-E. coli therapy can be attributed in part to the elicitation of tumor-specific cytotoxicity T cells, which can in turn provide durable anticancer immunity following bacterial clearance.
evidence: This is an inference from the CD8+ T cell depletion and tumor rechallenge studies.

claim: E. coli possesses great tumor-targeting ability following intravenous injection in mice due to the hypoxic and immune-suppressive tumor microenvironment.
source: It has been reported that E. coli possesses great tumor-targeting ability following intravenous injection in mice due to the hypoxic and immune-suppressive tumor microenvironment.
evidence: This is established knowledge about E. coli tumor-targeting ability.

claim: The combination of E. coli and oxaliplatin synergistically suppresses tumor growth.
source: Our previous study has also shown that the combination of E. coli and oxaliplatin synergistically suppresses the tumor growth (Lim et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lim et al., 2024.

claim: All mice maintained over 90% of their weights and remained active and healthy during the course of treatments with systemic delivery of IroA-E. coli and oxaliplatin.
source: All mice maintained over 90% of their weights and remained active and healthy during the course of the treatments (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Intravenous injection of E. coli, either wild-type or IroA transformant, resulted in subdued anti-tumor efficacy compared to intratumoral injection.
source: Unlike the intratumoral injection, the intravenous injection of E. coli, either the wild-type or the IroA transformant, resulted in subdued anti-tumor efficacy (Figure 6c–e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6c-e.

claim: Oxaliplatin monotherapy only slightly inhibited tumor growth.
source: Also, the monotherapy of oxaliplatin only slightly inhibited the tumor growth.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: The combination of oxaliplatin with wild-type E. coli delayed tumor progression but did not achieve complete remission.
source: The combination of oxaliplatin with the wild-type E. coli delayed the tumor progression but did not achieve complete remission.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6d and e.

claim: The combination of oxaliplatin and IroA-E. coli significantly suppressed tumor growth and achieved complete remission in 1 out of 4 mice.
source: Remarkably, the combination of oxaliplatin and IroA-E. coli significantly suppressed the tumor growth and achieved complete remission in 1 out of 4 mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6d and e.

claim: The systemic delivery of IroA-E. coli was synergistic with oxaliplatin chemotherapy in mouse tumor models.
source: Overall, our data revealed that the systemic delivery of IroA-E. coli was synergistic with the oxaliplatin chemotherapy in the mouse tumor models.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: This work provides the first proteomic data comparing E. coli cultured in rich medium and colonized in mouse tumor.
source: This work provides the first proteomic data comparing E. coli cultured in the rich medium and colonized in the mouse tumor.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study.

claim: The proteins involving 'the de novo synthesis of IMP' are highly enriched in E. coli grown in tumors compared to the rich medium condition.
source: For example, the proteins involving 'the de novo synthesis of IMP' are highly enriched in the E. coli grown in tumors compared to the rich medium condition.
evidence: This is an observation from the proteomic data analysis.

claim: When the environment is deficient of purine, bacteria need to synthesize them using de novo pathways.
source: Inosine phosphate (IMP) is the precursor of purine. When the environment is deficient of purine, the bacteria need to synthesize them using de novo pathways (Rolfes and Zalkin, 1988; Cho et al., 2011; Meng et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rolfes and Zalkin, 1988, Cho et al., 2011, and Meng et al., 1990.

claim: Genes associated with de novo purine synthesis are the most critical factors for the growth of E. coli or other gram-negative bacteria in human serum.
source: A previous report by Samant et al. has shown that the genes associated with the de novo purine synthesis are the most critical factors for the growth of E. coli or other gram-negative bacteria in human serum (Samant et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Samant et al., 2008.

claim: Humans control purine at a very low level in blood as a strategy of nutritional immunity to restrain bacterial proliferation.
source: Their data indicate that, similar to iron, humans also control the purine at a very low level in blood as a strategy of nutritional immunity in order to restrain the proliferation of bacteria.
evidence: This is an inference from the cited work by Samant et al., 2008.

claim: Bacteria and cancer cells vie for growth within the TME.
source: Given that bacteria and cancer cells vie for growth within the TME, an enhanced bacterial adaptation to the TME may potentially improve the anti-tumor activity.
evidence: This is a general statement about the competitive relationship in the TME.

claim: An enhanced bacterial adaptation to the TME may potentially improve anti-tumor activity.
source: Given that bacteria and cancer cells vie for growth within the TME, an enhanced bacterial adaptation to the TME may potentially improve the anti-tumor activity.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic strategies.

claim: The cured mice established durable anti-tumor adaptive immunity.
source: Notably, the cured mice have also established durable anti-tumor adaptive immunity.
evidence: This is supported by tumor rechallenge experiments.

claim: 1128 protein IDs were identified in E. coli from tumors.
source: The Venn diagram of the E. coli protein IDs identified in the rich medium and in the tumor microenvironment (TME).
evidence: This is shown in the Venn diagram in Figure 1a indicating 1128 total proteins in tumor (25 unique + 1103 shared).

claim: 1798 protein IDs were identified in E. coli from rich medium (LB).
